```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`networkPlot` takes a network built by `networkGen` and produces two things:
its **pathway enrichment** and its **interactive HTML rendering** (plus
kinase-by-pathway heatmaps). This vignette covers the inputs, the
enrichment call, reading the pathway output, and every knob on the HTML.

```{r setup}
library(networkPlot)
```

## 1. Inputs

Everything starts from a `networkGen` result -- its `nodes` and `edges`
data frames. `nodes` carries `Protein`, `type` (`Kinase` for the input
kinases, `Hidden` for the Steiner connector nodes PCSF added), `prize`,
`LogFC` (the kinase statistic), `degree`. `edges` carries `from`, `to`,
`weight` (how many of the randomized PCSF runs kept the edge) and `cost`
(the reference PPI's interaction cost -- lower = a stronger interaction).

```{r toy}
nodes <- data.frame(
  Protein = c("BRAF", "RAF1", "MAP2K1", "MAP2K2", "MAPK1", "MAPK3", "AKT1", "STEINER1"),
  type    = c(rep("Kinase", 7), "Hidden"),
  prize   = c(0.95, 0.9, 0.85, 0.7, 0.8, 0.75, 0.6, 2),
  LogFC   = c(2.4, 1.8, 1.2, 0.9, 1.1, 0.6, -0.8, 0),
  degree  = c(3, 3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1, 3)
)
edges <- data.frame(
  from = c("BRAF", "RAF1", "MAP2K1", "MAP2K2", "MAPK1", "STEINER1"),
  to   = c("MAP2K1", "MAP2K2", "MAPK1", "MAPK3", "STEINER1", "AKT1"),
  weight = c(8, 7, 8, 5, 3, 6),
  cost   = c(0.08, 0.12, 0.05, 0.30, 0.45, 0.10)
)
```

## 2. Enrichment

`enrich_network()` tests the network's **input kinases** for
over-representation in each pathway; **connector nodes** (PCSF `Hidden`
nodes, SIGNOR bridges -- see `network_roles()`) are never tested, because
they are not drawn from the UKA kinase list.

- **Pathway set:** Reactome v2 (`reactome_v2_pathway_table()`), Reactome cut
  at a curated depth per top-level category, bundled with the package.
  Mutant/defect pathways that only duplicate their normal counterpart are
  left out (`include_disease = "specific"`, see `filter_disease_pathways()`),
  judged with the run's own kinase universe.
  Any table with `pathway_id`, `pathway_name`, `uniprot` can be passed as
  `pathway_table`.
- **Background:** the kinases UKA can predict (`ukadb_kinases()`),
  optionally restricted to the network's interactome (`interactome_ids`),
  that belong to at least one tested pathway (>= 3 such kinases).
- **Test:** one-sided Fisher, `p = phyper(k - 1, K, N - K, n, lower.tail =
  FALSE)`, Benjamini-Hochberg over the tested pathways.

```{r enrich}
res <- enrich_network(nodes)
```

`res$all` holds every tested pathway with p < 0.1; `res$short` the selected
pathways, one per hit list (the smallest p; the others with the same hits in
`also_matches`):

```{r enrich-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(head(res$short[, c("pw_name", "category", "n_hits", "hits", "pw_size_ukadb", "p_value", "fdr", "in_selector")], 3),
             digits = 4, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Selected pathways, one per hit list (first 3 rows)")
```

Pass `out_dir` and `label` (e.g. `label = "DrugA_vs_DMSO_spec0.7"`) to also
write, to a `Network_pathways` subfolder of `out_dir`:
`pathways_<label>_all.csv` (tested pathways with p < 0.1),
`pathways_<label>.csv` (one pathway per hit list) and
`pathways_<label>_pw_params.csv` (background size, pathway set, selector
rule, ...). `networkGen`'s own output (`nodes_*`/`edges_*`/...) lands
directly in that same `out_dir`.

`enrich_uka()` runs the same enrichment on UKA data directly, without a
network: per comparison it takes the input kinases exactly as networkGen
selects them for a network (`networkGen::uka_top()`) and writes the same
CSVs to a `UKA_pathways` subfolder. `plot_uka_pathway_heatmaps()` draws its
result.

## 3. Reading the pathway output

Columns: `pw_id`, `pw_name`, `category` (top-level Reactome category),
`n_hits` (k) and `hits` (the tested kinases in the pathway, `;`-joined),
`pw_size_ukadb` (K, the pathway's background kinases), `p_value`, `fdr`,
`in_selector` (p < 0.05 and >= 3 hits; when more than 20 pass, also FDR <
0.3) and, in the one-per-hit-list table, `also_matches`.

`plot_pathway_heatmaps(comparisons, out_dir)` (or the folder wrapper
`plot_pathway_heatmaps_dir()`) draws the selected pathways with their hit
kinases, filled with the kinase statistic. The default `"wrapped"` layout
gives one small panel per pathway, wrapped into rows: one figure per
comparison, and one per pair of comparisons with the pathways selected in
both (`pair_groups`: only pairs within one group, e.g. a UKA Supergroup). `layout = "classic"` draws pathway x kinase heatmaps per comparison
and across comparisons.

## 4. The interactive HTML

`plot_network()` returns a `visNetwork` htmlwidget -- printing it (or, as
here, just letting it be the chunk's last value) embeds the live,
interactive network right in this page. Plotting `res$nodes` (from the
enrichment step above, so it carries the `pathway` column) turns on the
pathway multi-select dropdown -- try it:

```{r plot}
w <- plot_network(
  res$nodes, edges, title = "DrugA vs DMSO",
  theme = networkplot_theme(edge_width = list(column = "cost", invert = TRUE))
)
w
```

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
save_network_html(w, "results/DrugA", "DrugA_vs_DMSO.html") # -> results/DrugA/Network_html/DrugA_vs_DMSO.html
```

`save_network_html()` always writes into a `Network_html` subfolder of the
output folder you give it -- kept separate from `networkGen`'s own output
(`nodes_*`/`edges_*`/`wc_df_*`/`missing_nodes_*`) and `enrich_network()`'s
`pathways_*` CSVs, which all land directly in that same folder with no
subfolder of their own.

### Where the theme lives

Every visual choice is a field on the list `networkplot_theme()` returns,
passed as `theme =`. Calling it with no arguments gives the standard look;
override a field by name to change just that one thing.

```{r theme}
th <- networkplot_theme(
  shapes     = c(Kinase = "diamond"),            # merged over the defaults
  edge_width = list(column = "cost", invert = TRUE)  # thicker edge = stronger interaction
)
names(th)
```

Tunable HTML features and their theme fields:

| Feature | Field(s) |
|---|---|
| node shape per `type` | `shapes` (merged over the default map), `shape_default` |
| node fill = diverging `LogFC` scale | `logfc_palette`, `logfc_limit_fn` |
| high-degree node highlight | `highlight_degree`, `highlight_border`, `border_default`, `highlight_border_width`, `border_width_default` |
| edge colour | `edge_colour` |
| **edge boldness** | `edge_width` -- `NULL` for constant, or `list(column, scale, invert)`; use `column = "cost", invert = TRUE` for interaction strength, or `column = "weight"` for run-frequency robustness |
| fonts | `node_font_size`, `legend_font_size` |
| layout | `layout`, `seed` |

The pathway multi-select dropdown and the node-search box are always on;
the dropdown appears whenever `nodes` has a `pathway` column and
`colour_by = "pathway"` (the default).

## 5. End to end, in one call

Enriching and plotting is almost always done together, so
`enrich_and_plot_network()` wraps both steps -- call it once and get both
results back (same result as sections 2 and 4 combined, so not re-run here):

```{r e2e, eval = FALSE}
out <- enrich_and_plot_network(
  nodes, edges, title = "DrugA vs DMSO",
  theme = networkplot_theme(edge_width = list(column = "cost", invert = TRUE))
)
save_network_html(out$widget, "results/DrugA", "DrugA_vs_DMSO.html")
```

Call `enrich_network()` and `plot_network()` separately instead of the
wrapper when you already have an enrichment result from elsewhere.
